content.text: {"relation": "DIVERGENT", "consensus_summary": "All three blind responses converge on a two-part core: righteousness is primarily (1) right standing before God — in the dominant Protestant framing, God's righteousness imputed/credited to the believer through faith in Christ apart from works (Gen 15:6; Rom 3:21-26; 4:3-8; Phil 3:9; 2 Cor 5:21) — and (2) conformity to God's moral character and will that flows from that status. Recognized alternatives include infused/transformative righteousness, ethical conduct as such, covenant faithfulness, social justice, and Christ himself as righteousness, but the forensic-relational 'gift received by faith, not earned by works' reading anchors the consensus primary in every response.", "book_summary": "The book identifies righteousness as the actual doing of God's commandments — the law kept and worn as a garment of righteous acts — and explicitly denies the two things the consensus centers on: it is 'not a vague goodness nor a verdict only received.' Its common-view note names imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works precisely as the view it rejects. Proof texts are Deut 6:25 ('it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments'), Ps 119:172 ('all thy commandments are righteousness'), and 1 John 3:7 ('he that doeth righteousness is righteous').", "consensus_core_identification": "Righteousness = right standing with God granted/credited through faith in Christ apart from works (forensic-relational status), together with the moral conformity to God's standard that flows from it.", "book_core_identification": "Righteousness = the performed keeping of God's commandments — righteous acts done, constituting the garment of righteousness — with explicit denial that righteousness is a received verdict or imputed status.", "core_relation": "CONTRADICTS", "extension_relation": "PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION", "boundary_disagreement": "The consensus admits both status-cases (a believer declared righteous by faith prior to or apart from performed works, e.g., Abraham in Gen 15:6, the ungodly justified in Rom 4:5) and conduct-cases (righteous acts). The book excludes the status-cases entirely: no one is righteous by a credited verdict; only doers of the commandments are righteous. Conduct-cases are retained and made the whole extension.", "material_contradiction": "The consensus primary asserts righteousness is 'counted apart from works' and received as a verdict by faith (Rom 4:3-8; Phil 3:9); the book asserts righteousness is constituted by doing the commandments and is expressly 'not a verdict only received.' Both cannot be true of the same term in the same salvific context: if righteousness just is performed obedience, then imputed righteousness apart from works is not righteousness at all. The book's own common-view note frames the consensus reading as the position it denies.", "rationale": "This is more than boundary refinement. Although the book's positive content coincides with the 'ethical/behavioral righteousness' alternative that all three responses list as common, the book does not offer it as one sense among several — it makes commandment-keeping the exclusive identification and explicitly negates the forensic-imputed core that every blind response places at the center (and that the book itself acknowledges as the common teaching). Accepting the book requires rejecting the consensus's central identification (a gift-status received by faith apart from works) and replacing it with achieved obedience. That is replacement of the central referent, not narrowing within it, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the doing-based reading is recognizable within the consensus's alternatives (1 John 3:7 is cited on both sides).", "citation_support": "STRONG", "strongest_objection": "One could argue for REFINED instead: the consensus itself spans status and conduct, and every response lists ethical/practiced righteousness (with 1 John 3:7) as a common alternative; the book could be read as merely narrowing the term's extension to the conduct half rather than replacing the referent. On this view the disagreement is over which recognized sense is primary, which the rubric might treat as boundary/precision disagreement rather than material contradiction. The counter is that the book's explicit 'not a verdict only received,' aimed directly at the consensus's named primary, is a denial of the consensus identification, not a re-weighting of it.", "confidence": "medium"}
